This is Viglet Turing Search, an open source plugin for WordPress and WooCommerce. In the next few minutes I'll put it on a WordPress shop that has never had it, connect it to Viglet Turing, index the catalog, and show what the shop and its owner get from it.
It installs like any other plugin. Under Plugins, Add New, I upload the release zip and install it. The same package also works from Composer.
Activated. It adds one menu, Viglet Turing Search, and everything it does lives under it: settings, setup, fields, health, tuning and insights.
The Setup page asks for four things: the address of your Turing, an API key created in Turing, the name of the Semantic Navigation site, and the language the content is written in.
[pleased] It tests every step on the way: the address, the network, Turing itself, the key, and the site. This site didn't exist yet, so one click created it, with the fields the plugin needs.
By default it indexes posts and pages. This one is a shop, so under Settings, Indexing, I turn on products as well.
Saved. Categories, tags and custom fields can go in the same way, and the Fields page maps each content type's fields.
Back on Setup, the first index sends every published item of those types, in batches, with its progress on screen.
Done. The whole catalog and its guides are in Viglet Turing. From now on, a new or edited post is sent on its own, in the background.
Over on the storefront, the search block now asks Viglet Turing. I'll type a plain search.
[upbeat] Results, with filters built from the shop's own fields: category, stock, colour, size and price. Nobody had to configure those by hand.
And the owner sees what visitors look for, under Insights.
The search I just made is already counted. Top searches, searches that found nothing, and results nobody opened: each one tells the shop what to fix next.
That's the whole setup: a zip, a key and one index. The code is on GitHub, the documentation is on the Viglet site, and the demo store runs right in your browser, with nothing to install.
